# Longitudinal biomarkers {#sec-b13}



::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## At a glance

**Guiding question:** Whose course does the estimated slope describe?\
**For:** clinical researchers, doctoral students and reviewers who work with repeated laboratory values ·
**Prerequisites:** estimands (@sec-b02), missing values and denominators (@sec-b03), simple linear regression\
**In the course:** [W5 · Causality, trajectories and phenotypes](https://r-heller.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r-course/lessons/w5-causality-trajectories-phenotypes.html) ·
**Data:** synthetic (generated in the chapter; [download as CSV](../data/b13-selenium-synthetic.csv)) ·
**Core reading time:** about 10 minutes
:::

## Case and decision {#sec-b13-case}

A doctoral researcher in a fictitious spinal cord injury centre has serum selenium values from 36 people after
traumatic spinal cord injury: one sample at admission and up to five more over the following eight weeks. Before the
next research meeting, the supervising consultant asks a single question. Does selenium recover more slowly after a
complete injury than after an incomplete one? If it does, the team will draft a protocol for a supplementation trial
restricted to people with complete injuries. Published observational work on trace elements after spinal cord injury
motivates the question [@seelig2020selenium]; every value in this chapter is *synthetic*. Not everybody stayed for all
visits. Some people were transferred, others missed late appointments. Whether the protocol is justified therefore
depends on a question that sounds technical but is clinical: whose course does the estimated slope describe?

## Core reading {#sec-b13-core}

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Core reading** · required for W5 · about 10 minutes · ends before ‘Lab’
:::



**One table, three levels.** A longitudinal data set has three levels that are easily confused: the person, the visit
and the measurement. Here, 36 people (18 per injury group) were due to be sampled six times, at admission and at
weeks 1, 2, 4, 6 and 8. That gives 216 planned values; 186 were measured. The independent unit is the
person. Any statement about "the course after a complete injury" is a statement about people, so its uncertainty must
be driven by the number of people, not by the number of tubes in the freezer.

**The quantity of interest.** The consultant's question concerns a time–group interaction: the difference between
the mean change per week after a complete injury (ASIA Impairment Scale grade A) and after an incomplete injury
(grades B–D). Its unit is µg/L per week. A value of −1 means that selenium rises by 1 µg/L per week less after a
complete injury. The difference at admission is a separate quantity, the group main effect, and answers a different
question.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Serum selenium (µg/L, *synthetic*) over eight weeks after traumatic spinal cord injury. Thin grey lines: one person each; thick line: fitted mean course of the group from the mixed model. The numbers along the bottom are the persons measured at each visit. n = 36 persons (18 per group), 186 of 216 planned measurements.](b13-longitudinal-biomarkers_files/figure-html/fig-b13-spaghetti-1.png){#fig-b13-spaghetti fig-alt='Two side-by-side panels, incomplete injury on the left and complete injury on the right. The horizontal axis shows weeks since admission at 0, 1, 2, 4, 6 and 8; the vertical axis shows serum selenium in micrograms per litre. Each panel contains thin grey lines for individual persons and one thick line for the group mean. The mean rises by about 1.6 micrograms per litre per week in the incomplete group and by about 0.6 in the complete group. Persons measured at each visit fall from 18 to 17 in the incomplete group and from 18 to 10 in the complete group.' width=1050}
:::
:::


**What the figure shows.** @fig-b13-spaghetti draws one thin line per person (a spaghetti plot) and the fitted mean
course of each group. In the complete-injury group, the denominator falls from 18 at admission to
10 at week 8; in the incomplete group it falls to 17. People with low
values left more often. The people still visible at week 8 are therefore not a random subset of those admitted.

**Three answers to one question.** @tbl-b13-estimates compares three ways of estimating the interaction.

- *Pooled regression.* One straight line per group through all measured values, as if every measurement came from a
  different person. It ignores that values from the same person are correlated, so its interval is too narrow for a
  statement about people, and it lets persons with many visits dominate. Here, the late visits come mostly from people
  with a better course, and the estimated difference shrinks towards zero.
- *Slope per person (baseline).* For each person with at least two values, fit a straight line and keep its slope;
  then compare the mean slope between groups. This summary-measure approach [@matthews1990serial] is the biometrically
  sensible baseline: transparent, person-based and easy to check by hand. It weights a person with two values like a
  person with six, and it silently drops people with a single value.
- *Linear mixed model.* A model with a random intercept and a random slope per person [@laird1982random], fitted with
  **lme4** [@bates2015lme4]. Each person gets their own line, but lines from people with few values are pulled
  towards the group mean. All 36 persons and all measured values enter.


::: {#tbl-b13-estimates .cell tbl-cap='Difference in the weekly change of serum selenium, complete minus incomplete injury (µg/L per week, *synthetic*), with 95% confidence intervals. The simulation truth is known only because the data were generated in the chapter.'}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|Approach                                |Units used                     | Difference| Lower 95%| Upper 95%|
|:---------------------------------------|:------------------------------|----------:|---------:|---------:|
|Pooled regression (ignores persons)     |186 measurements               |      -0.54|     -1.33|      0.25|
|Slope per person (baseline)             |33 persons                     |      -1.13|     -1.92|     -0.34|
|Mixed model, random intercept and slope |36 persons, 186 measurements   |      -0.99|     -1.67|     -0.31|
|Simulation truth                        |36 persons, 216 planned values |      -1.00|          |          |


:::
:::


Because the data are synthetic, the true difference (−1.0 µg/L per week) is known. In this cohort, the pooled
regression underestimates the difference, the per-person slopes overestimate it and the mixed model comes closest.
One cohort proves nothing about a method; the counter-check repeats the experiment a hundred times
(@sec-b13-countercheck).

**Whose course?** The three numbers describe different people. The pooled slope is the course of the
*measurements*, and late measurements come from those who stayed. The mean of per-person slopes describes everybody
with at least two values, each counted once, however noisy their line. The fixed slope of the mixed model describes a
typical admitted person – under one condition.

**The most important assumption.** **The mixed model's slope describes everyone who was admitted only if the chance of
leaving the study depends on what had already been measured, not on the unmeasured current value or on the person's
own unobserved rate of recovery.** This condition is called missing at random (MAR) [@rubin1976inference]. In the
simulation, transfers depend on the last measured selenium value, a stand-in for the observable clinical condition,
so MAR holds by construction. In a real cohort, it is an assumption that no analysis of the observed data can prove.
When leaving depends on what was not observed (missing not at random, MNAR), every estimate in
@tbl-b13-estimates can be biased, and the honest response is a sensitivity analysis
[@diggle1994informative; @little2012missing]. The mechanisms are explained in more depth in the
[Methods in R lab on MCAR, MAR and MNAR](https://r-heller.github.io/methods-in-r/sec-ch-16-design.html#sec-chapters-16-design-labs-lab-mcar-mar-mnar).

**What to say in the meeting.** A defensible sentence would be: "In 36 people, selenium rose by about
1.0 µg/L per week less after a complete injury (mixed model, 95% CI
0.3 to 1.7). This assumes that leaving the study depended on
observed values. If the people who left had values about 18 µg/L higher than their own
earlier course predicts, the difference would disappear." The last sentence comes from the sensitivity analysis in
the lab. It turns a hidden assumption into a number that the clinical team can judge.

**Question for the workshop.** Which observable reason for leaving the study – transfer to intensive care, death,
discharge home, a missed outpatient appointment – would make the MAR assumption more plausible, and which less? Sort
the four reasons before you open the lab.

## Lab {#sec-b13-lab}

The lab runs in a fresh R session in about ten seconds. It needs **lme4** and **ggplot2**.

### Step 1: write down the simulation assumptions

Every number in the simulation is an *assumption* that is set here and nowhere else. The dropout rule makes the
chance of leaving before the next visit depend on the last measured value (MAR). A second rule, used only in the
counter-check, makes it depend on the unmeasured current level and on the person's own recovery rate (MNAR).


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(1313)                                     # set again so this chunk always gives the same cohort
n_per_group <- 18                                  # persons per injury group
weeks <- c(0, 1, 2, 4, 6, 8)                       # planned visits, weeks since admission
true_start <- c(incomplete = 62, complete = 58)    # mean selenium at admission (µg/L)
true_slope <- c(incomplete = 1.6, complete = 0.6)  # mean change (µg/L per week)
sd_start <- 7                                      # between-person SD at admission (µg/L)
sd_slope <- 0.6                                    # between-person SD of the weekly change (µg/L per week)
sd_noise <- 4                                      # measurement and day-to-day noise (µg/L)

simulate_cohort <- function(mechanism = c("mar", "mnar", "none")) {
  mechanism <- match.arg(mechanism)
  ids <- sprintf("P%02d", seq_len(2 * n_per_group))
  group <- rep(names(true_start), each = n_per_group)
  dev_start <- rnorm(length(ids), 0, sd_start)     # each person's deviation at admission
  dev_slope <- rnorm(length(ids), 0, sd_slope)     # each person's deviation of the weekly change
  d <- data.frame(id = rep(ids, each = length(weeks)),
                  group = rep(group, each = length(weeks)),
                  week = rep(weeks, times = length(ids)))
  p <- match(d$id, ids)
  d$true_level <- true_start[d$group] + dev_start[p] + (true_slope[d$group] + dev_slope[p]) * d$week
  d$selenium <- d$true_level + rnorm(nrow(d), 0, sd_noise)
  d$observed <- TRUE
  for (k in seq_along(ids)) {                      # monotone dropout: once gone, always gone
    r <- which(d$id == ids[k])
    for (j in 2:length(r)) {
      linear_predictor <- switch(mechanism,
        none = -Inf,
        mar  = -2.8 - 0.2 * (d$selenium[r[j - 1]] - 60),               # last measured value
        mnar = -2.8 - 0.2 * (d$true_level[r[j]] - 60) - 1.5 * dev_slope[k] / sd_slope)  # unmeasured state
      if (runif(1) < plogis(linear_predictor)) {
        d$observed[r[j:length(r)]] <- FALSE
        break
      }
    }
  }
  d$group <- factor(d$group, levels = c("incomplete", "complete"))
  d
}

cohort_full <- simulate_cohort("mar")              # all planned visits, with the observed flag
cohort <- cohort_full[cohort_full$observed, c("id", "group", "week", "selenium")]
n_persons <- length(unique(cohort$id))
n_week8 <- table(cohort$group[cohort$week == 8])   # persons still measured at week 8
stopifnot(nrow(cohort_full) == 216, n_persons == 36,
          all(table(cohort$id[cohort$week == 0]) == 1))  # everybody has an admission value
```
:::


### Step 2: document the denominators at person level

Before any model, count people, not rows. @tbl-b13-persons gives the denominator for every visit and the number of
people who contribute at least two values (needed for a per-person slope).


::: {#tbl-b13-persons .cell tbl-cap='Persons with a measurement at each visit, by injury group (*synthetic*). The last two columns count persons with at least two measurements and all measurements of the group.'}

```{.r .cell-code}
per_visit <- as.data.frame.matrix(table(cohort$group, cohort$week))
n_meas_person <- table(cohort$id)
group_of_id <- tapply(as.character(cohort$group), cohort$id, unique)
per_visit$`persons with ≥ 2 values` <- as.vector(tapply(n_meas_person >= 2, group_of_id, sum)[rownames(per_visit)])
per_visit$`all measurements` <- as.vector(table(cohort$group)[rownames(per_visit)])
names(per_visit)[1:6] <- paste("week", weeks)
knitr::kable(per_visit)
```

### Step 3: three estimates of the interaction


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(lme4)
ctrl <- lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")
# (1) Pooled regression: every measurement treated as if it were a separate person (a common mistake)
fit_pooled <- lm(selenium ~ week * group, data = cohort)

# (2) Baseline: one least-squares slope per person with at least two values
per_person <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(cohort, cohort$id), function(d) {
  if (nrow(d) < 2) return(NULL)
  data.frame(id = d$id[1], group = d$group[1], n_values = nrow(d),
             slope = unname(coef(lm(selenium ~ week, data = d))["week"]))
}))
welch <- t.test(slope ~ group, data = per_person)   # Welch test; estimates are incomplete, complete

# (3) Linear mixed model: random intercept and random slope for every person
fit_lmm <- lmer(selenium ~ week * group + (week | id), data = cohort, REML = TRUE, control = ctrl)
summary(fit_lmm)$coefficients
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

#> (Intercept)        63.6672802  1.5549897 40.943860
#> week                1.6025084  0.2190990  7.314082
#> groupcomplete      -8.1093780  2.2107271 -3.668195
#> week:groupcomplete -0.9926302  0.3458073 -2.870472
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
VarCorr(fit_lmm)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

#>  id       (Intercept) 6.00271         
#>           week        0.68483  -0.083 
#>  Residual             4.07563
```


:::
:::


The coefficient `week` is the mean weekly change after an incomplete injury (µg/L per week); `week:groupcomplete` is
the interaction, the amount by which the weekly change differs after a complete injury.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
est_pooled <- unname(coef(fit_pooled)["week:groupcomplete"])
ci_pooled <- unname(confint(fit_pooled)["week:groupcomplete", ])
est_person <- unname(welch$estimate[2] - welch$estimate[1])      # complete minus incomplete
ci_person <- -rev(unname(welch$conf.int))
est_lmm <- unname(fixef(fit_lmm)["week:groupcomplete"])
ci_lmm <- unname(confint(fit_lmm, parm = "week:groupcomplete", method = "Wald")[1, ])
fmt <- function(x) cdsr_number(x, 2)
estimates_table <- data.frame(
  Approach = c("Pooled regression (ignores persons)", "Slope per person (baseline)",
               "Mixed model, random intercept and slope", "Simulation truth"),
  `Units used` = c(paste(nrow(cohort), "measurements"), paste(nrow(per_person), "persons"),
                   paste(n_persons, "persons,", nrow(cohort), "measurements"), "36 persons, 216 planned values"),
  Difference = c(fmt(est_pooled), fmt(est_person), fmt(est_lmm), fmt(-1)),
  `Lower 95%` = c(fmt(ci_pooled[1]), fmt(ci_person[1]), fmt(ci_lmm[1]), ""),
  `Upper 95%` = c(fmt(ci_pooled[2]), fmt(ci_person[2]), fmt(ci_lmm[2]), ""),
  check.names = FALSE)
estimates_table
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>                                  Approach                     Units used
#> 1     Pooled regression (ignores persons)               186 measurements
#> 2             Slope per person (baseline)                     33 persons
#> 3 Mixed model, random intercept and slope   36 persons, 186 measurements
#> 4                        Simulation truth 36 persons, 216 planned values
#>   Difference Lower 95% Upper 95%
#> 1      -0.54     -1.33      0.25
#> 2      -1.13     -1.92     -0.34
#> 3      -0.99     -1.67     -0.31
#> 4      -1.00
```


:::
:::


The target values below are fixed for this seed. They guard against silent changes in the data or the packages.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
stopifnot(
  nrow(cohort) == 186, nrow(per_person) == 33,           # measured values and persons with >= 2 values
  !isSingular(fit_lmm),                                  # both random-effect variances estimated
  abs(est_lmm - (-1)) < 0.1,                             # mixed model close to the truth in this cohort
  est_pooled > est_lmm, est_person < est_lmm,            # pooled shrinks, per-person slopes exaggerate
  ci_lmm[1] < -1, ci_lmm[2] > -1                         # interval covers the simulation truth
)
```
:::


::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Fitting `lm(selenium ~ week * group)` to all rows treats 186 tubes as 186 people. The standard error then reflects the
number of measurements, not the number of independent persons, and persons with many visits dominate the slope. The
same pseudoreplication appears with spectra per animal (@sec-b10) and steps per walk (@sec-b11).
:::

### Step 4: sensitivity analysis for late and missing visits

Two analyses test how much the answer depends on the visits that were not made.

*(a) Early slope only.* Refit the mixed model with weeks 0–4, where most people are still present. If the
interaction changes markedly, the conclusion rests on the late visits of a selected group.

*(b) Delta adjustment and tipping point.* Fill every missing planned visit with the mixed model's prediction for that
person (the MAR value), shift the filled values by δ µg/L, and refit. A positive δ means that people who left were
doing better than their own earlier course predicts (for example, discharged home after a good recovery); a negative
δ means they were doing worse. The tipping point is the δ at which the group difference vanishes. Filling in a single
value per visit understates the uncertainty, so only point estimates are reported here; for intervals, use multiple
imputation (see the
[CTTIR lab on multiple imputation with mice](https://cttir.github.io/courses/course3_design_causal/labs/lab_week2_session2.html)).


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
fit_early <- lmer(selenium ~ week * group + (week | id), data = subset(cohort, week <= 4), control = ctrl)
est_early <- unname(fixef(fit_early)["week:groupcomplete"])

missing_visits <- cohort_full[!cohort_full$observed, c("id", "group", "week")]
mar_value <- predict(fit_lmm, newdata = missing_visits)   # person-specific prediction (uses random effects)
refit_with_delta <- function(delta) {
  filled <- rbind(cohort, data.frame(missing_visits, selenium = mar_value + delta))
  unname(fixef(lmer(selenium ~ week * group + (week | id), data = filled, control = ctrl))["week:groupcomplete"])
}
delta_grid <- seq(-8, 24, by = 4)
delta_est <- vapply(delta_grid, refit_with_delta, numeric(1))
tipping_delta <- uniroot(refit_with_delta, interval = c(0, 40))$root
missing_by_group <- table(missing_visits$group)
data.frame(delta = delta_grid, interaction = round(delta_est, 2))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>   delta interaction
#> 1    -8       -1.43
#> 2    -4       -1.21
#> 3     0       -0.99
#> 4     4       -0.77
#> 5     8       -0.55
#> 6    12       -0.33
#> 7    16       -0.11
#> 8    20        0.11
#> 9    24        0.33
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
c(early_only = round(est_early, 2), tipping_point_delta = round(tipping_delta, 1))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

#>               -1.45               18.10
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
stopifnot(nrow(missing_visits) == 216 - nrow(cohort),
          tipping_delta > 0,                                        # the difference vanishes only for delta > 0
          missing_by_group[["complete"]] > missing_by_group[["incomplete"]])
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(data.frame(delta = delta_grid, interaction = delta_est), aes(delta, interaction)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = cdsr_linetypes[[2]], colour = cdsr_colours[["grey"]]) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = est_lmm, linetype = cdsr_linetypes[[4]], colour = cdsr_colours[["blue"]]) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = tipping_delta, colour = cdsr_colours[["red"]]) +
  geom_line(colour = cdsr_colours[["blue"]], linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(colour = cdsr_colours[["blue"]], shape = cdsr_shapes[[1]], size = 2.2) +
  annotate("text", x = tipping_delta, y = min(delta_est), hjust = 1.05, size = 3.2,
           label = paste0("tipping point: δ = ", cdsr_number(tipping_delta, 1), " µg/L")) +
  labs(x = "Assumed shift δ of missing values (µg/L)", y = "Interaction (µg/L per week)",
       caption = "Single conditional-mean imputation; point estimates only.") +
  theme_cdsr()
```

With weeks 0–4 only, the interaction is -1.45 µg/L per week (all visits:
-0.99). The tipping point lies at δ = 18.1 µg/L
(@fig-b13-delta), about 4.5 times the assumed measurement noise. Most filled
visits belong to the complete-injury group (25 of 30), so
optimistic assumptions about the people who left move this group's slope upwards and the difference towards zero.
Whether a shift of this size is plausible is a clinical judgement, not a statistical one. It should be made before
the data are seen, by people who know why patients leave this kind of unit.

**If the result stays unclear.** When the tipping point lies within the range that clinicians find plausible, the
honest summary is that the data do not settle the question. Report the MAR estimate, the tipping point and the
reasons for leaving; do not search for the analysis that gives the desired answer. The next study can record
reasons for missed visits, add a home or outpatient sample at week 8 and fix the sensitivity range in the analysis
plan.

## Counter-check {#sec-b13-countercheck}

Change the dropout mechanism and keep everything else. **Predict first:** (1) If nobody drops out, will the three
approaches agree? (2) Under MAR dropout, which approach is unbiased on average? (3) If leaving depends on the
unmeasured current level and on the person's own recovery rate (MNAR), in which direction will the mixed-model
estimate move? Then run one hundred cohorts per mechanism. The simulation follows the logic of Monte Carlo experiments
with explicit assumptions (see [Strategy in R: law of large numbers and Monte Carlo](https://r-heller.github.io/strategy-in-r/sec-probability.html#law-of-large-numbers-and-monte-carlo)).


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(1300)
n_rep <- 100
n_singular <- 0                                   # singular fits are counted, not hidden
estimate_all <- function(obs) {
  per <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(obs, obs$id), function(d)
    if (nrow(d) >= 2) data.frame(group = d$group[1], slope = coef(lm(selenium ~ week, data = d))[["week"]])))
  m <- suppressMessages(lmer(selenium ~ week * group + (week | id), data = obs, control = ctrl))
  if (isSingular(m)) n_singular <<- n_singular + 1
  c(pooled = coef(lm(selenium ~ week * group, data = obs))[["week:groupcomplete"]],
    per_person = diff(tapply(per$slope, per$group, mean))[[1]],
    mixed = fixef(m)[["week:groupcomplete"]])
}
replicates <- lapply(c(none = "none", mar = "mar", mnar = "mnar"), function(mech)
  t(replicate(n_rep, { d <- simulate_cohort(mech); estimate_all(d[d$observed, ]) })))
summary_rep <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(replicates), function(mech) {
  r <- replicates[[mech]]
  data.frame(mechanism = mech, approach = colnames(r), mean = colMeans(r),
             mc_se = apply(r, 2, sd) / sqrt(n_rep))
}))
rownames(summary_rep) <- NULL
summary_rep$mean <- round(summary_rep$mean, 2); summary_rep$mc_se <- round(summary_rep$mc_se, 3)
summary_rep
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

#> 1      none     pooled -0.95 0.029
#> 2      none per_person -0.95 0.029
#> 3      none      mixed -0.95 0.029
#> 4       mar     pooled -0.81 0.044
#> 5       mar per_person -1.34 0.072
#> 6       mar      mixed -1.02 0.036
#> 7      mnar     pooled -0.83 0.035
#> 8      mnar per_person -0.93 0.071
#> 9      mnar      mixed -0.89 0.032
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
m_of <- function(mech, appr) summary_rep$mean[summary_rep$mechanism == mech & summary_rep$approach == appr]
stopifnot(
  max(abs(replicates$none[, "pooled"] - replicates$none[, "mixed"])) < 1e-6,   # complete data: identical
  max(abs(replicates$none[, "per_person"] - replicates$none[, "mixed"])) < 1e-6,
  abs(m_of("mar", "mixed") - (-1)) < 0.1,          # MAR: mixed model unbiased within simulation error
  m_of("mar", "pooled") > -0.9,                     # MAR: pooled estimate attenuated
  m_of("mnar", "mixed") > m_of("mar", "mixed")      # MNAR: mixed model moves towards zero
)
```
:::


The results answer the three predictions. With complete data, all three approaches give identical estimates in
every cohort: in a balanced design, the mixed model's fixed slope equals the pooled and the per-person slope. Under
MAR dropout, the mixed model is unbiased on average (-1.02 against −1.00), the pooled regression is
pulled towards zero (-0.81) and the per-person slopes are pushed away from it
(-1.34), because people who leave after a low value contribute short, steep lines. Under MNAR,
the mixed model also drifts towards zero (-0.89): it can only use what was observed. In
11 of 300 fits, the random-slope variance was estimated at the boundary; these fits are counted
and kept. The lesson for the consultant's question is that agreement between baseline and mixed model is reassuring
only when few visits are missing. Disagreement is a signal to examine the reasons for leaving.

## Consequences for patients and operations {#sec-b13-consequences}

**Patients and ethics.** The people who left were mostly from the complete-injury group, and they had low values. They
are exactly the people a supplementation trial would target, and the estimate is least certain for them. A protocol
should not rest on a slope that describes the people who managed to come back. Each extra blood draw is a burden for
people with a new spinal cord injury; the next study should place samples where care already happens (ward rounds,
rehabilitation visits) and record every reason for a missed visit. A group-level slope is a research finding, not an
individual prognosis, and should not be communicated to patients as one (@sec-b21).

**Data protection.** A small cohort with a rare injury level, age, sex and exact visit dates can identify a person even
without a name. The CSV file of this chapter is synthetic. With real data, share weeks since admission rather than
dates, pseudonymised IDs and only the variables needed for the analysis; the questions of access and re-use are
treated in @sec-b23 and @sec-b26.

**Regulation and security.** A slope used as a research end point does not make the analysis a medical device. The
question would arise if software computed individual recovery forecasts from biomarker courses and clinicians used
them to choose a treatment; @sec-b22 sets out how intended purpose drives that classification. Information security is
indirectly relevant: the analysis data set, the code and the package versions must be versioned so that the numbers in
the meeting can be reproduced (@sec-b04).

## Look up and transfer {#sec-b13-lookup}

**Reviewer question.** How many persons, not measurements, contribute to the late part of each group's course, and how
far does the interaction move under a plausible MNAR scenario?

**Self-test.** A second synthetic cohort studies zinc after spinal cord injury. Here, people who recover well are
discharged home after week 4 and their week-6 and week-8 values are missing; people who do poorly stay on the ward.
In which direction is the pooled regression biased for the group with most discharges, and what would a sensitivity
analysis need to assume?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The late measurements now come from people with a poorer course, so the pooled slope of the group with most
discharges is too flat. The mixed model under MAR corrects this only as far as the early values already reveal who is
recovering well. If discharge depends on improvement that was not yet measured, the data are MNAR, and the mixed model
is also too flat for that group. A sensitivity analysis would shift the missing late values upwards (positive δ) and
report the δ at which the conclusion changes. Recording the reason "discharged home" makes the mechanism visible.
:::
